2d109ae8fcf200c533bafe8f8e630a4d04ee98b4.text: Improves on #12105 by using the shard shape as `previous_chunks` instead of `chunks`, giving larger, shard-aligned chunks. Thanks @dcherian for noting `auto_chunks` nearly always concatenates `previous_chunks`, but not always, risking shard-misalignment when global config's memory limit is below shard size. Should we raise an exception when config and shard shape compete, prompting the user to change config?

2d5ab5f9280f89734c632ccde00b31f6e5804f4e.text: This improves on #12105 by taking the shard shape and using it as the `previous_chunks` parameter, rather than using `chunks` for that role as before. The effect of doing it this way is that the rechunking ends up producing larger chunks which are nevertheless still shard-aligned. Thanks are due to @dcherian for reminding me of the fact that `auto_chunks` nearly always ends up concatenating the `previous_chunks` argument that it is given. But that is not something that happens every single time. Because of that, this change introduces the possibility of chunks that are shard-misaligned, specifically in the case where the global configuration declares a memory limit that is smaller than the shard size itself. So what exactly should we do in the situation where there is competition between the global config on one side and the shard shape of the zarr array on the other? Would raising an exception be the appropriate response here, one that prompts the user to go and change their config?

## Summary

Fixes #3972

The `no-duplicate-selectors` rule will now correctly go and detect duplicate class selectors in the case where they happen to use different CSS escape sequence formats. As an example of this, `.u-m\00002b` and `.u-m\+` are now recognized as being duplicates of one another, and this is because both of them actually represent `.u-m+`.

## Changes

- Added a `normalizeNodeEscaping()` helper over in `normalizeSelector.mjs`, one which makes use of postcss-selector-parser's getter/setter behavior in order to normalize the CSS escaping
- Added some test cases specifically for the escaped selector duplicates

## How it works

The fix leverages the built-in value getter/setter behavior that postcss-selector-parser provides for the ClassName nodes. The getter goes and returns the unescaped value, while the setter, for its part, re-escapes that value into a normalized form instead. So, simply by going ahead and doing `node.value = node.value`, we go and trigger this whole normalization process, which is what then ensures that equivalent selectors will end up comparing as equal to each other, regardless of what their original escape format happened to have been.

Reference: https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/blob/1b1e9c3bc10ccc3bc5f07a987caa7f2684c0b52f/src/selectors/className.js#L13-L28

## Summary

Fixes #3972

The `no-duplicate-selectors` rule is now able to correctly go ahead and detect the duplicate class selectors in exactly those cases where they happen to make use of different CSS escape sequence formats from one another. As a concrete example of what is meant by this, the two selectors `.u-m\00002b` and `.u-m\+` are now going to be recognized as being duplicates of one another, and the underlying reason for that is because both of them are, in actual fact, representing the very same thing, namely `.u-m+`.

## Changes

- Added in a brand new `normalizeNodeEscaping()` helper function, going ahead and placing it over inside of the `normalizeSelector.mjs` file, and this is a helper which goes ahead and makes use of the particular getter/setter behavior that belongs to postcss-selector-parser, doing so specifically and deliberately in order to be able to normalize the CSS escaping that happens to be present in the selectors
- Added in a whole number of new test cases as well, ones that are there specifically and particularly for the case of the escaped selector duplicates that this is meant to handle

## How it works

The particular way that the fix here goes about working is that it goes and leverages the built-in value getter/setter behavior that postcss-selector-parser happens to have available for the ClassName nodes in particular. The getter, for its own part on its side of things, goes ahead and returns right back the unescaped value, whereas the setter, for its own part on its side of things, goes ahead and re-escapes that same value into a properly normalized form instead. And so, simply by going ahead and doing `node.value = node.value`, what it is that we manage to accomplish is to trigger off this whole entire normalization process, and the net effect that comes out of that is to ensure that any equivalent selectors there may be are going to end up comparing as being fully equal to one another, and, moreover, that this particular fact holds true completely and totally regardless of whatever their own original escape format may happen to have been in the very first place to begin with.

Reference: https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/blob/1b1e9c3bc10ccc3bc5f07a987caa7f2684c0b52f/src/selectors/className.js#L13-L28

b6f9e003c95f1880bf079782a720b300f8a4c41c.text: This change is an improvement on the earlier #12105, and the way it improves on it is by taking the shard shape and passing that in as the value of the `previous_chunks` parameter, rather than passing in `chunks` for that purpose the way that it was being done before. The practical result that comes out of making this particular substitution is that the rechunking operation ends up producing chunks that are larger in size, while at the very same time those same larger chunks still manage to remain properly shard-aligned. I want to extend my thanks to @dcherian for taking the time to remind me of the important detail that `auto_chunks` will, in nearly all of the cases that come up in practice, go ahead and concatenate the `previous_chunks` argument that has been handed to it. That said, it is worth being clear and explicit that this is not something which holds true in absolutely every single case that can arise. It is precisely because of that caveat that this change opens up the possibility of ending up with chunks that are shard-misaligned, and this can happen specifically in the scenario where the global configuration goes and declares a memory limit whose value happens to be smaller than the size of the shard. This naturally raises a question worth asking: what is it that we ought to do in the particular situation where there turns out to be direct competition between, on the one hand, the global config, and on the other hand, the shard shape of the zarr array in question? Would it perhaps be an appropriate thing for us to raise an exception at that particular point in time, an exception whose whole and entire purpose would simply be to prompt the user into going ahead and changing their own config accordingly so as to suit the particular situation at hand?

### Context

This adds a brand new security check for GCP Compute Engine, one whose job is to detect any and all VM instances that happen to be configured with multiple network interfaces on them. The concern here, the reason it matters, is that VMs which have multiple NICs are able to act as bridges sitting right between networks that are really and truly supposed to remain fully isolated from one another, and this potentially ends up allowing attackers to move laterally, going from one network segment across to another one.

### Description

This PR goes ahead and adds a new GCP check, one that verifies whether or not the Compute Engine instances happen to have multiple network interfaces that are configured on them. The check goes through and carefully evaluates every single one of the VM instances that there are, and then, once done, it reports back to the user the following set of results:

* **PASS**: the instance in question has just a single network interface on it
* **FAIL**: the instance in question has multiple network interfaces on it (that is to say, 2 or more of them in total)

**Note**: instances that happened to be created by GKE, or else that are being used in the role of network virtual appliances, may quite legitimately and genuinely have a real need for multiple network interfaces on them.

### Context

This adds a brand new security check for GCP Compute Engine, one whose job is to ensure that the custom disk images are not being publicly shared with anyone at all. The reason that this matters so much is that images which have ended up being publicly shared are able to go and end up exposing sensitive data, or proprietary software, or even quite specific infrastructure details, and to do all of that exposing directly to unauthorized users, which is something that goes on to create some genuinely significant security risks.

### Description

This PR goes ahead and adds a new GCP check, one that verifies whether or not the Compute Engine custom disk images happen to have any IAM bindings on them that end up granting public access. The check goes through and evaluates every one of the custom images, and then it reports back the following results:

* **PASS**: the image in question is not being publicly shared with anyone at all
* **FAIL**: the image in question is being publicly shared out with `allAuthenticatedUsers`

**Note**: according to the GCP documentation, `allUsers` cannot actually be granted any roles on images, and so, because of that, only `allAuthenticatedUsers` is the one that ends up being checked here.

#### Changes include:

**Compute Service (`compute_service.py`):**
- Added an `images` list, one that is there to store the custom image data
- Added a `_get_images()` method, one that goes and does the following set of things in turn: it lists out all of the custom images that there are by way of a call to `images().list()`; it then retrieves the IAM policy for each one of the images by way of a call to `images().getIamPolicy()`; and finally it extracts out the public members (that is to say, the `allAuthenticatedUsers`) from out of the bindings that it got back
- Added an `Image` model of its own, one that comes along with a `public_members` field sitting on it

**New Check (`compute_image_publicly_shared/`):**
- The check logic itself, which goes and evaluates the public sharing for each and every image
- A Metadata JSON file, one that comes with remediation guidance included
- Unit tests, ones that go and cover the images both with and without public sharing on them

### Steps to review

1. Review the `Image` model that was added over to `compute_service.py`

The real, underlying concern that sits behind the whole of all of this is the fact that VMs which happen to have multiple NICs on them are, precisely as a direct result of that, able to go and act in the capacity of bridges that end up sitting right there in between networks which are genuinely and truly supposed to be kept fully, completely, and properly isolated from one another at all times, and the real danger that comes out of that is that this potentially ends up opening the door to allowing attackers to go and move laterally, making their way from one network segment across and over into another separate one that they were never intended to be able to reach in the very first place at all.

### Description

What it is that this PR actually does is go right ahead and add in a brand new GCP check, one whose entire purpose is to verify whether or not the Compute Engine instances happen to have multiple network interfaces that are configured on them. * **PASS**: the instance in question here happens to have only just a single, solitary network interface configured on it, and nothing more than that
